newsitem.title: CHINA: More children allowed into HK under Beijing deal.
newsitem.headline: More children allowed into HK under Beijing deal.

text.p: Beijing and Hong Kong on Wednesday agreed to allow more mainland-born children into the territory, a senior immigration official said.

But Hong Kong Immigration Director Regina Ip, in Beijing to discuss a crisis over a growing number of illegal child immigrants from China, said the two sides had not agreed on the size of the increase. "It is difficult to determine at this stage the extent of the increase because any increase will obviously eat into the sub-quotas allocated for other categories," Ip said.
"So the Public Security Ministry (of China) will undertake an overall review and they will come to a decision at the end of the year," she said in comments carried on Hong Kong media.

Hong Kong's Basic Law, the new constitution in effect since China resumed control of the former British colony on July 1, allows mainland-born children the right of abode if they have a parent with legal residency rights in the territory.

At present, 66 children are allowed to move to Hong Kong each day. Hong Kong wants to raise the quota to 90, but that would be over half the current overall quota of 150 for people of all ages and categories.
With a backlog of 66,000 children, thousands of young illegal immigrants have sneaked in to avoid the slow legal route.

Last week, Hong Kong passed a tough law to deport the child illegals, even if they ultimately have the right of abode, fearing there would be an even bigger influx if they were allowed to stay after jumping the queue.
The law also set up a system whereby Hong Kong would issue a "certificate of eligibility" to be used in combination with a "one-way permit" issued by China.
Ip said the first batch of 500 certificates were handed to authorities in Guangdong province adjacent to Hong Kong on Wednesday.
"We will be handing over more in the next few weeks and are expecting the first batch of children holding these certificates affixed to one-way permits to arrive in early August," she said.
Families with children facing deportation have vowed to fight the new law, and many have applied for and won legal aid enabling them to face the government in court.
